pages.page_summary: The page concludes the discussion on work by noting that non-conservative work depends on the path. It introduces Section 5.10, defining power as the rate of work done, providing formulas for average and instantaneous power, and listing units like Watts and Horsepower. It includes Example 5.10 regarding elevator power. Section 5.11 introduces collisions, describing a scenario where a moving mass collides with a stationary mass, illustrated by a diagram showing the resulting trajectories.
knowledge_points: Non-conservative work (Wnc) depends on the particular path from i to f.
Power is defined as the time rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
Average power (Pav) is the ratio of work (W) to total time (t).
Instantaneous power (P) is the limiting value of average power as the time interval approaches zero.
Instantaneous power can be expressed as P = F · (dr/dt) or P = F · v.
Power is a scalar quantity with dimensions [ML²T⁻³].
The SI unit of power is the watt (W), which is equivalent to 1 J s⁻¹.
The unit of power is named after James Watt, an innovator of the steam engine.
A 100-watt bulb running for 10 hours consumes 1 kilowatt hour (kWh) of energy.
kWh is a unit of energy, not power.
Example 5.10 calculates the power required for an elevator carrying 1800 kg moving at 2 m/s against a 4000 N frictional force.
Collisions involve the application of laws of momentum and energy conservation.
In a collision between a moving mass m1 and a stationary mass m2, the masses fly off in different directions.
The relationship between masses, velocities, and angles in a collision is a subject of study.

visuals.description: A 2D coordinate system diagram illustrating a collision. A blue dot labeled m1 moves horizontally from left to right along the x-axis with velocity vector v1i. It collides with a grey dot labeled m2 located at the origin. After the collision, m1 moves diagonally up and to the right with velocity vector v1f, making an angle θ1 with the x-axis. m2 moves diagonally down and to the right with velocity vector v2f, making an angle θ2 with the x-axis. Dashed lines indicate the paths of the masses after the collision.
visuals.educational_role: Illustrates the geometry of a two-dimensional collision between a moving object and a stationary object, defining the variables (masses, velocities, angles) used in the subsequent analysis.
